passage: In Noor's Class 6 dance club at the community centre, Hafsa, the instructor's assistant, showed a new step. Noor copied it twice, then looked at her feet. Later she stayed behind as everyone packed up. "Miss Hafsa, how did you learn to spin so fast?" she asked. Hafsa laughed. "Falling a lot." Noor's eyes widened. "You fell?" "Every week, for a year." Noor tied her hair the same way as Hafsa's, in a low braid over the shoulder. Next week she wore a similar red band and asked for Hafsa's advice on turning. Hafsa said, "I still get it wrong sometimes. Don't wait for perfect." Noor grinned.

qa.q: How did Hafsa say she learned to spin so fast?
qa.a: She said she learned by falling a lot, every week for a year.

qa.q: What does Noor's copying of Hafsa's braid and red band suggest she feels toward Hafsa?
qa.a: It suggests Noor admires Hafsa and wants to be like her. It may also show she wants to belong to the dance club.

qa.q: How can a young admirer keep her admiration healthy?
qa.a: She can learn from the effort behind the skill, as Hafsa described, and remember that her hero also makes mistakes.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel about Noor's admiration?
qa.a: Hafsa may feel pleased and a little responsible. Her honesty about still getting it wrong shows she doesn't want to be seen as flawless.

grounding: A child looks up to an older teacher, copies her style, and learns that admiration needs balance because heroes are not flawless.

passage: Vaibhav's little cousin Yamini had one poster on her wall of a woman cricketer. He noticed she hummed while combing her hair, and had started holding her bat with the same low grip. "She never misses a practice," Yamini told him proudly. "She wakes up at five." Then she set the alarm for five, though she was asleep by nine and cranky at breakfast. After two days she said, "I read that even she got dropped from the team once." She studied the poster for a while and kept the alarm at six. Vaibhav couldn't tell whether she was disappointed or relieved.

qa.q: What time did Yamini first set her alarm for?
qa.a: She first set her alarm for five.

qa.q: What might Yamini have felt when she learned her hero had been dropped from the team, and what else could Vaibhav's uncertainty mean?
qa.a: She may have felt surprised and perhaps a little comforted that her hero is not flawless. Vaibhav couldn't tell if she was disappointed or relieved, so it could be both.

qa.q: What could Yamini do to learn from her hero without copying everything?
qa.a: She could copy the habits that suit her, like regular practice, and pick a wake-up time that keeps her rested.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav see Yamini's admiration?
qa.a: Vaibhav watches with affection and some caution, noticing both her effort and her crankiness. He is unsure what she feels about the news.

grounding: A child admires a sports star and copies her style, and admiration is balanced when she learns the hero is not flawless.

passage:
Monday: Ayesha came home and put her hair in a tight bun, just like Damini Ma'am's. She practised writing her capital A with the same curly tail. "Ma'am says my handwriting is improving," she told Ammi, glowing.
Wednesday: In maths, Ma'am wrote a sum on the board, and it was wrong. Ravi said so. Ma'am's cheeks went pink. Ayesha stared at her book. She felt oddly let down, as if a wall had cracked.
Friday: Ma'am began class by saying, "On Wednesday I made a mistake, and Ravi was right to say so. Teachers get things wrong too." Ayesha looked up. That night she still wore the bun. But she told Ammi, "Ma'am said sorry to the whole class. I want to be brave like that."

qa.q: Whose bun did Ayesha copy?
qa.a: Damini Ma'am's.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling when she stared at her book on Wednesday?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and unsettled, because the teacher she admired had made a mistake, as if a wall had cracked.

qa.q: How did Damini Ma'am's choice on Friday help Ayesha?
qa.a: By admitting the mistake openly, she showed that a hero can be wrong and still be worth copying, which gave Ayesha a more balanced admiration.

qa.q: How might Ravi have felt when Ma'am said he was right?
qa.a: Ravi likely felt relieved and respected, since pointing out a teacher's mistake can feel risky.

grounding: Across a week, a child admires and copies a teacher, sees her make a mistake, and learns admiration can include flaws.

passage:
"Jasleen, you keep copying that singer's hairstyle. Let me, your Tushar Mamu, tell you something. When I was your size in Jalandhar, I worshipped a fast bowler from our state team. I copied his long run-up, his collar turned up, even the way he spat on the ball. I practised in the lane till the neighbours shouted.
Then one day he came to our town for a camp. I stood in the line with my autograph book for two hours. When my turn came, he signed without looking and snapped at the boy behind me. My heart just sank.
For a week I didn't bowl. Then I thought, his run-up is still good, even if his manners weren't. So I kept the run-up and dropped the collar."

qa.q: How long did Tushar stand in the autograph line?
qa.a: Two hours.

qa.q: What was young Tushar feeling when the bowler snapped at the boy?
qa.a: He felt hurt and disillusioned, because his hero was rude and didn't live up to the picture he had of him.

qa.q: What choice inside the story helped Tushar keep growing?
qa.a: He chose to keep copying the bowler's good run-up while dropping the parts he no longer admired, instead of giving up bowling.

qa.q: How might the boy behind Tushar in the line have felt?
qa.a: That boy probably felt shocked and small, having waited just as long only to be snapped at by his hero.

grounding: An uncle recalls admiring a sports star, being disappointed by him, and learning that heroes are not flawless.

passage:
Nikita wanted everything like her big sister Shreya: the same high ponytail, the same way of hooking her thumbs in her pockets, the same roller skates one day. Today Shreya had a skating practice across town, and Nikita begged to come.
It poured all afternoon. The bus was packed and they stood squashed by the door, Nikita holding Shreya's bag like treasure.
At the rink, Shreya tried her new jump and fell hard. She sat on the floor, rubbing her hip, and snapped at the coach. Nikita's mouth fell open. Shreya never fell.
On the ride home, Shreya was quiet. Then she said, "I fall all the time, you know. You just don't see it."
Nikita thought about that. Then she whispered, "I still want to learn."

qa.q: What did Nikita hold on the crowded bus?
qa.a: Shreya's bag, like treasure.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling when Shreya fell and snapped at the coach?
qa.a: Nikita felt shocked, because she had believed Shreya never fell or got cross; she may also have felt worried for her sister's hip.

qa.q: What would you advise Nikita about admiring her sister?
qa.a: Keep learning from Shreya's skill and practice, but remember that she makes mistakes and has bad days like anyone else.

qa.q: What is it like for Shreya to be admired so much?
qa.a: It may feel nice, but also like pressure, since she has to admit she falls all the time and isn't perfect.

grounding: On a rainy trip to a skating rink, a child who copies her admired sister sees her fall and learns heroes are not flawless.

passage: Ujjwal copied everything Indu didi did. He tied his laces in her double knot, spun his racket before serving the way she did, and told the whole colony his sister was the best badminton player in Lucknow. On Saturday he went to watch her district match. Indu lost the second game badly, threw her towel down and snapped at her coach. Ujjwal's chest felt tight. In the auto home he asked in a small voice, "Didi, were you being rude?" Indu looked out at the traffic. "I was. I was angry at myself and took it out on him. I'll say sorry tomorrow." Ujjwal thought for a while. Then he spun his racket anyway. "You're still the best. Just not every minute." Indu laughed.

qa.q: Which city did Ujjwal say his sister was the best badminton player in?
qa.a: Lucknow.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal's chest feel tight during the match?
qa.a: He felt upset and confused seeing his hero lose her temper, which didn't fit the flawless picture he had of her.

qa.q: What helped Ujjwal keep admiring Indu in a healthier way?
qa.a: Asking her directly and hearing her admit the mistake and plan an apology, so he could see she is great but not perfect.

qa.q: How might Indu have felt when Ujjwal asked if she was being rude?
qa.a: She likely felt ashamed of snapping, but also respected his honesty enough to admit it plainly.

grounding: It shows a child whose admiration for an older sibling drives copying and praise, and who learns that a hero can make mistakes.
